strengths: The core idea is interesting and timely: leveraging affordance-aware textual descriptions from a VLM as contextual knowledge to guide a diffusion prior for 3D hand pose refinement under occlusion is a novel combination, and the paper convincingly motivates why affordances (object category, shape, size, interaction type, intention, grasp taxonomy) are richer contextual cues than prior coarse signals (verbs, captions, intention labels).

The two-step description generation pipeline (parsed caption extraction via QwenVL2.5 followed by LLM summarization, inspired by chain-of-thought prompting) is a sensible engineering design and is a reusable contribution.

The strongest empirical claim — a 4.9 mm (25%) PA-MPJPE reduction under high occlusion (11+ occluded joints) versus HaMeR, and 4.9/2.6 mm versus the text-free InterHandGen baseline — directly supports the central hypothesis that contextual affordance reasoning helps most where it should help most (heavily occluded joints).

The refinement scheme is well designed: selectively refining only occluded joints (self-occlusion via ray casting, object occlusion via SAM2 mask overlap) while anchoring visible joints to 2D keypoint evidence is a reasonable and interpretable strategy.

The controllability analysis (Fig. 5, varying object size while fixing grasp taxonomy) is a nice qualitative demonstration that the conditioning carries semantic information beyond a nuisance variable.
The paper is clearly written, with a well-motivated introduction, an understandable method section, and informative figures.
weaknesses: Ground-truth leakage at test time: the paper explicitly states that VLM classification of grasp taxonomy is unreliable, so the ground-truth grasp taxonomy annotations from HOGraspNet are used to supply accurate taxonomy information for the framework. Since grasp taxonomy is the key pose-defining element of the affordance description, this means a quantity strongly correlated with the evaluation target (the ground-truth hand pose) is given to the model at inference. This substantially weakens the claim that the VLM-derived contextual descriptions drive the improvement, and the reported gains cannot be attributed fairly to the proposed pipeline in a realistic deployment setting. At minimum, an ablation with the VLM-predicted (noisy) taxonomy is required to quantify this.

Very small and possibly insufficient evaluation: results are reported on only 300 sampled instances (one-tenth subsampling of the dataset), with no variance, confidence intervals, or significance testing. The headline average improvement over HaMeR is only 0.23 mm (8.51 to 8.28 mm), which is plausibly within noise on such a small sample; only the high-occlusion bin shows a convincing gain. The experiment design does not support the claim of 'consistent' improvement across occlusion levels with statistical confidence.

Limited evidence for the causal role of the descriptions: there is no ablation over description components (e.g., with/without grasp taxonomy, with/without intention, shuffled or random descriptions, GT annotations vs. VLM-generated descriptions vs. no descriptions). Without these, one cannot tell whether the gains come from the rich affordance content specifically or simply from any conditioning signal interacting differently with the occlusion-aware refinement schedule (nr scaled by occlusion count).

Modest methodological novelty relative to prior work: the diffusion architecture is adapted from InterHandGen (replacing counter-hand conditioning with CLIP text features), the refinement strategy follows [16], and the setup (HaMeR initial estimates, 2D keypoint fitting, diffusion-based refinement) is established. The main novelty is the conditioning signal, so the paper leans heavily on the affordance idea — making the missing ablations and the GT-taxonomy leakage more consequential.

Narrow evaluation scope: only PA-MPJPE on one dataset (HOGraspNet) and one initial estimator (HaMeR) is reported. No comparison to other contextual or diffusion-refinement methods (e.g., G-HOP, score-guided diffusion [22], physics-based [30]), no MPJPE/AUC metrics, no evaluation of the description generation pipeline itself (e.g., accuracy of VLM-extracted elements against GT annotations), and no cross-dataset or in-the-wild generalization test.

Training and implementation details are sparse: the training data, number of training poses, training compute, inference cost of the refinement loop, and prompt templates are not described, which harms reproducibility. It is also unclear how the method behaves when affordance descriptions are wrong or partially incorrect, which will be the common case outside benchmark settings.

Qualitative claims of 'more natural and physically plausible' grasps (Fig. 4) are supported only by vertex error heatmaps and no user study or physical plausibility metrics (e.g., penetration, contact alignment with the object).
No limitations discussion or societal-impact considerations are provided.

strengths: The motivation is compelling and well-articulated: using affordance knowledge (object shape, function, grasp type) to resolve occlusion ambiguity in 3D hand reconstruction is an interesting and underexplored direction, and the paper is to the authors' credit the first to bring affordance-aware textual descriptions into this task.

The two-stage VLM captioning pipeline (structured element extraction followed by LLM summarization, motivated by chain-of-thought reasoning) is a sensible design choice for producing fine-grained affordance descriptions.

The occlusion-aware refinement strategy is thoughtful: selectively refining only occluded joints (detected via ray casting for self-occlusion and SAM2 masks for object occlusion) while fixing visible joints is a reasonable way to avoid degrading already-correct estimates.

The reported improvement under high occlusion (21.3mm to 16.4mm, ~25%) is substantial, and the qualitative controllability results (Fig. 5, changing object size alters grasp aperture) nicely demonstrate that the textual conditioning carries semantic signal.
The paper is generally clearly written and the method pipeline (Figs. 2-3) is easy to follow.
weaknesses: Ground-truth leakage at test time: the paper admits that classifying grasp taxonomy with VLMs is 'highly challenging' and therefore relies on ground-truth taxonomy annotations from HOGraspNet to supply the grasp type in the affordance description. This is a serious fairness issue: at test time the method consumes an oracle annotation that encodes exactly the kind of hand-pose information the task is supposed to recover. The comparison against HaMeR and the text-free InterHandGen baseline is thus not apples-to-apples, and the practical utility of the method in a true single-RGB-image setting is unvalidated.

The headline average improvement is marginal: 8.51mm to 8.28mm is a 0.23mm reduction, which is likely within run-to-run/sample noise. The paper reports no variance, confidence intervals, or significance testing, and evaluates on only 300 sampled instances, so the claim of 'consistently outperforming' regression methods is weakly supported.

The experimental evidence is very thin for the claims made: a single dataset (HOGraspNet), a single initial estimator (HaMeR), a single adapted baseline (InterHandGen without one-hand conditioning), and no comparison to any other contextual/semantic-conditioning or occlusion-refinement method (e.g., G-HOP, diffusion-based recovery [22, 30], or promptable approaches [25]).

Limited novelty in methodology: the diffusion prior architecture is explicitly derived from InterHandGen [12], the refinement scheme from [16], conditioning from CLIP, captioning from an off-the-shelf VLM. The contribution is essentially a combination of existing components with a new conditioning text; the paper would benefit from a more careful positioning of what is technically new versus reused.

Key ablations are missing: no ablation over the description elements (which of the six fields actually matter), no evaluation of the VLM captioning quality/accuracy on held-out images (particularly without GT taxonomy), no ablation of the occlusion-detection criteria, and no analysis of sensitivity to the noise level schedule n_r.

The evaluation is on one-tenth of the dataset with 300 test instances and the split protocol details are sparse; no training details (data size, epochs, hyperparameters), prompts, or code release are mentioned, which raises reproducibility concerns.

The paper is very short (4 pages of content) with a brief experiments section, no limitations discussion, no societal impact statement, and no failure analysis — well below the depth expected of a full-length ECCV submission.

Quantitative support for the 'functionally coherent' claim is absent: there is no grasp-classification accuracy or contact/penetration metric to substantiate that refined poses are more functionally plausible; only the qualitative examples in Figs. 4-5 support this.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and well-motivated problem: 3D hand pose estimation under severe self- and object-occlusion, and the idea of using affordance-aware textual descriptions as a contextual prior is interesting and, to my knowledge, a reasonably novel combination for this task.

The two-step description generation pipeline (VLM parsed captions + LLM summarization, inspired by chain-of-thought) is a sensible design for obtaining structured, fine-grained affordance descriptions and improves interpretability.

The selective refinement strategy (diffusing only occluded joints, detected via ray casting for self-occlusion and SAM2 mask overlap for object occlusion) is a thoughtful adaptation of score-guided diffusion refinement.

The gains under high occlusion (21.3 -> 16.4 mm PA-MPJPE, ~25%) are meaningful for the hardest cases, and the controllability analysis (Fig. 5) nicely demonstrates that the prior responds to affordance semantics such as object size.
The paper is clearly written, with a well-structured motivation distinguishing affordances from coarser contextual signals (verbs, captions, intention labels).
weaknesses: Ground-truth leakage at test time undermines the central claim: the paper states that classifying grasp taxonomy with VLMs is 'highly challenging' and therefore relies on the ground-truth annotations of HOGraspNet to supply taxonomy information. Since grasp taxonomy is a key element of the affordance description, a substantial part of the conditioning signal is derived from labels unavailable in a real deployment. The paper's framing as VLM-provided contextual knowledge at inference is therefore overstated; an experiment with VLM-predicted (imperfect) taxonomies, or an ablation excluding the taxonomy element, is needed to substantiate the claim.

The quantitative evidence is thin. Evaluation is on only 300 sampled instances of a single dataset, with a single initial estimator (HaMeR) and essentially one adapted baseline (InterHandGen with one-hand conditioning removed). No ablations are provided for the occlusion-detection criteria, the noise-level schedule nr, the choice of text encoder, or the contribution of individual description elements.

The headline average improvement is very small (8.51 -> 8.28 mm, i.e., 0.23 mm) and may be within evaluation noise given only 300 samples; no variance, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests are reported. The contribution rests almost entirely on the high-occlusion slice.

The methodological novelty is incremental: the diffusion architecture is adapted from InterHandGen, the refinement strategy from [16], and the conditioning uses off-the-shelf CLIP features. The main novel element is the affordance description conditioning, whose benefit is not isolated by a clean ablation (e.g., text-conditioned vs. text-free version of the authors' own model, rather than only the adapted IHGen baseline).

Several practical issues are unaddressed: the sensitivity of refinement to VLM description errors/hallucinations, the runtime cost of diffusion refinement relative to regression baselines, and behavior when the object mask (SAM2) or initial pose is poor. The paper is also short and lacks implementation details needed for reproducibility (training data details, hyperparameters, description templates).

The claim of being 'the first to introduce affordance-aware textual descriptions into 3D hand reconstruction' should be more carefully qualified relative to prior contextual/promptable approaches (e.g., G-HOP, PromptHMR, [29, 30]) which use related semantic signals.
